title: David-Horodok’s interwar institutions and the emigration of its people
summary: Banks, schools, libraries, political movements, and elections reveal a community building its institutions even as migration carried residents away.

editorialConnections.recordTitle: Young group takes over library management

editorialContent:
## Rebuilding a communal life

After the Polish-Bolshevik war, Jewish life in [David-Horodok](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_1ffa438353dc176e94f25c7d) began to rebuild amid economic hardship and political uncertainty. The memorial book recalls that organizations, parties, youth movements, cultural societies, and charitable institutions took shape, with young people bringing particular energy to their work. The account presents not one institution but a network: schools and libraries, political organizations, banks, and communal bodies that helped residents learn, debate, earn a living, and care for one another.

This revival followed years of upheaval. The memorial book says that the town’s earlier organizations had broken apart during war and revolution; some activists were arrested or fled, and others left during dangerous periods. After the fighting, education became an urgent concern. The [Tarbut School](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_b84fd472a05662a588932f2c) was reestablished in 1924, under the leadership of [R. Mishlov](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_81aae6d249451ac6c7461c05). The memorial book describes it as beginning with three classes and later expanding to seven, sustained largely by tuition and the commitment of teachers, parents, and supporters. It continued into 1940, though the Soviet takeover changed its language of instruction from Hebrew to Yiddish.

For young people drawn to Zionism and pioneering, [Z. S.](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_90bfa7569d261aea5affc727) founded [Ha-Halutz](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_737b792f28a95935681c5fc5) in David-Horodok in 1923, according to the memorial book. This founding is the focus of one record, which gives the year as 1923. The surviving account situates the movement within a wider political and cultural landscape: its organizations offered ways to prepare for life and work in the Land of Israel, while schools, libraries, and study groups helped sustain Hebrew and Jewish cultural life at home.

The book also describes earlier pioneering aspirations that met obstacles. Following the postwar upheaval, a group formed with the intention of immigrating to the Land of Israel, but the book says events there in 1921 halted aliyah and the group remained in town. That account helps explain why the 1923 founding of Ha-Halutz mattered locally: a movement could keep a collective aspiration alive even when departure was delayed. The memorial’s surviving passages do not give the names of Ha-Halutz’s founders or describe its full local program, so those details remain uncertain.

## Books, debate, and mutual support

In 1925, [Poalei Zion (T.S.)](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_0cecccf343d4802cd94c15a5) founded the [J. L. Peretz Library](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_af97ada338caf5e5f2cd423e), named for the writer [J. L. Peretz](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_0cc227bfee1981b8fa9f9bb7). It served adult readers; the Tarbut School had its own substantial student library. The memorial book describes readers, self-education groups, and amateur drama, a cultural life that crossed party lines and brought literature into public settings.

The library’s story also reveals how emigration reshaped local institutions. As many veteran activists made aliyah, the library faced a crisis. In 1935, a younger group took over its management. The memorial names [Kopel Moravchik](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_2d04e4e0140e605f38164369), [Chaim Moravchik](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_3cabaebbb40750afe844757a), [Chaim Farber](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_d3409091933429674f01d1ae), and [Zvi Shaklber](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_bc404a094ffb8f45f77d499b); its fuller account identifies Shaklber as the group’s head. The library revived, its readers grew in number, and new Yiddish, Hebrew, and Polish books were added. The record of the young group’s takeover thus marks both continuity and change: people left, but younger residents assumed responsibility for the institutions they had built.

Economic institutions were another part of communal life. The [Bank for Commerce](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_a33219ea619a8861ed770e45) was founded in 1923 under the management of [M. Kvitni](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_a837f9db7c7d649755b77503); the [People’s Bank](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_7fb72c45bdf0d2a4628559ff) followed in 1924 under [Sh. Papish](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_1dbe71ab55fa2f175fe1336f). These are management roles in the source, not evidence that either man employed the other or founded the bank alone. The memorial book later contrasts the banks’ experience during the 1933–1935 economic crisis: it says the merchants’ institution was forced to interrupt normal activity, while the People’s Bank continued more cautiously and met its obligations.

Political representation was contested too. The memorial book records that Jewish community-council elections took place in 1928 under Polish authorities, but the surviving excerpt does not provide results or candidate names. It would be misleading to infer who won or what the vote meant for any particular party.

## Leaving, staying, and the meaning of departure

Emigration was not a single movement or a simple choice. The memorial book’s account links departures to the aftershocks of war, restricted opportunities, and economic strain. It describes Jews leaving for Argentina, Cuba, and Canada, while others sought to reach the Land of Israel. The book does not provide a complete list of emigrants or a total number, and it does not establish the later fate of every family. Its account is a community recollection, not a comprehensive register of everyone who left or survived elsewhere.

The records preserve several different scales of departure: a pioneering group whose plans were interrupted; veteran library activists who made aliyah; and broader migration overseas. These movements changed the town even as its institutions endured. The younger people who revived the library in 1935 inherited more than books: they took on a civic and cultural responsibility left vulnerable by the departure of experienced members. Meanwhile, Ha-Halutz and the Tarbut School represented distinct but connected ways of preparing young people for a Jewish future—one oriented toward pioneering and aliyah, the other toward Hebrew education and communal culture.

Outside sources offer only limited independent checks on this particular story. Wikipedia’s entry for Davyd-Haradok confirms the town’s interwar Polish setting and notes its later wartime destruction, but it does not independently verify the local founding dates, named organizers, library succession, or destinations described here. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Davyd-Haradok?utm_source=openai)) Yad Vashem’s Encyclopedia of the Ghettos result concerns a different town, Gródek Jagielloński, not David-Horodok; it therefore adds no independent evidence about these interwar institutions or departures. ([wwv.yadvashem.org](https://wwv.yadvashem.org/yv/he/research/ghettos_encyclopedia/ghetto_details.asp?cid=208&utm_source=openai)) The specific evidence for the school, banks, library, election, and migration in this account comes from the memorial book, in JewishGen’s translation—not from independent confirmation.

The people named in the records bring the institutional story into focus: organizers and managers, educators, library stewards, and young activists. Yet the record remains incomplete. It does not identify most emigrants or trace the families who left. The story worth carrying forward is therefore both one of cultural vitality and of dispersal: people built institutions for a community in place, while many also chose—or hoped—to make lives elsewhere.
